Newborn Care

Asafoetida while breastfeeding: spice, remedies and safety

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Asafoetida, also called hing, is a strongly scented cooking ingredient and traditional remedy. Those uses raise different questions during breastfeeding. Reliable human evidence does not establish a milk-boosting benefit or a safe medicinal dose. Serious poisoning has followed direct administration to infants; that is a reason never to give babies an asafoetida remedy, not proof that a parent's normal seasoned meal causes the same exposure through milk.

What is asafoetida?

Asafoetida is a dried gum-resin obtained from Ferula plants and sold as pieces or powder, sometimes blended with other ingredients. It gives food a powerful onion- or garlic-like flavour. A food product, concentrated extract, capsule and homemade medicinal mixture can have very different contents and amounts; the familiar name alone does not identify the exposure.

These are large perennial plants with divided basal leaves, later upright stems, yellow umbrella-shaped flower clusters and seed-bearing fruits. Resin is collected from the plant, particularly its root region. Traditional uses also include young shoots or leaves as food or animal feed, roots in food preparations and pest-deterrent uses. This botanical history does not establish that every species, plant part or preparation is edible or suitable during lactation; do not identify or prepare wild plants from a brief description.

Traditional benefits are not established breastfeeding treatments

Traditional claims include digestive relief for gas, abdominal discomfort, bowel changes, stomach acid and parasites; respiratory relief for cough or bronchitis; and anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial or antioxidant effects. Laboratory activity or a history of use does not demonstrate that taking a commercial remedy safely treats an infection, IBS or another illness in a breastfeeding person.

Other claims involve memory loss or neurological and mental-health problems, fatigue, headache, back or dental pain, eyesight, liver health, skin ageing, corns or insect bites, fertility, sexual function and early ejaculation. These are not established indications for self-treatment with asafoetida during lactation. Traditional descriptions of a warming or drying quality are not clinical measures of effectiveness. Persistent symptoms need their own assessment, not a promise that one herb treats many conditions.

Does it increase breast milk?

There is no dependable human evidence establishing asafoetida as an effective and safe galactagogue, a substance intended to increase milk production. Neither traditional enthusiasm nor conflicting opinions establish a benefit. No standardized medicinal dose or duration can be recommended for breastfeeding on the available evidence.

If supply seems low, arrange a feeding assessment, including attachment, effective and frequent milk removal, infant weight and age-appropriate wet nappies. Illness, medicines and other maternal or infant factors may need attention. A lactation specialist can help make an individual plan, including supplemental feeding when medically needed. Do not postpone help or necessary infant nutrition while trying an herb; a crying baby alone does not prove low supply.

Milk transfer and direct infant poisoning are different

Reliable human data measuring asafoetida constituents in breast milk and their effects on nursing infants are lacking in the evidence reviewed here. It is therefore inaccurate to present transfer through milk causing infant bleeding as an established scientific finding. Limited information also cannot prove that concentrated maternal remedies are safe. NHS guidance advises against herbal medicines while breastfeeding because safety is insufficiently known.

Published case reports describe infants given asafoetida directly as a remedy, including for colic, developing methemoglobinemia: an abnormal form of haemoglobin that impairs oxygen delivery. Reports from 1984 and a report published online in 2019, in a 2020 journal issue, concern direct ingestion, not a demonstrated breast-milk pathway. This is not simply a bleeding disorder. Never put asafoetida into a baby's mouth, milk or bottle or use it as a home colic treatment.

Seasoning food is not taking a concentrated remedy

A small culinary amount in an adult meal is a different exposure from swallowing resin, extracts, capsules or repeated medicinal mixtures. There are not adequate lactation studies to assign an exact safe amount or certify every food product. Check the whole ingredient list for blends and your own allergies. General breastfeeding nutrition guidance supports a varied diet rather than unnecessary blanket food restrictions.

If you already ate a normally seasoned meal, do not assume your baby has been poisoned or automatically stop breastfeeding or discard milk. If a concentrated preparation, a large or uncertain amount, an unknown blend or symptoms are involved, contact a clinician, pharmacist or poison service promptly with the package, amount and timing. Advice depends on the actual exposure, infant age and health, including prematurity; do not improvise a waiting period before feeding.

Adverse effects, interactions and product uncertainty

Digestive upset or a skin reaction after a product warrants stopping the remedy and seeking advice if symptoms persist or worsen. Lists of headache, dizziness, altered alertness, agitation, urinary discomfort, low blood pressure or seizures do not establish how often asafoetida causes these effects, or a safe dose below which none occur. Significant new symptoms deserve assessment rather than being accepted as a harmless herbal effect.

Ask a pharmacist about all ingredients and medicines, especially anticoagulants, blood-pressure treatments, seizure medicines or an underlying bleeding disorder. Proposed herb interactions and laboratory effects are not quantified risks for every product, but uncertainty is a reason for caution. Do not stop prescribed treatment or substitute another supposedly safe herb. Natural origin, traditional use and marketing claims do not guarantee purity, accurate strength or breastfeeding safety.

When to seek help and how to plan next steps

If a baby has been given asafoetida as a remedy or may have swallowed a concentrated product, seek emergency medical advice immediately, even before symptoms. Blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing difficulty, a seizure, severe unusual drowsiness or loss of consciousness require immediate emergency care in either parent or baby. Sudden tongue or throat swelling with breathing or swallowing difficulty is also an emergency. Do not induce vomiting or give a home antidote; bring the packaging and follow the emergency team's instructions.

Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies than expected for age, poor weight gain, unusual bruising or bleeding, or persistent symptoms need prompt clinical assessment; do not diagnose the cause from a spice exposure alone. Discuss the reason for wanting a remedy and treatments compatible with breastfeeding with your care team. Keep medicinal products out of children's reach. A symptom record can support that discussion but must never delay care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish culinary food use, concentrated maternal remedies and direct infant administration.

Preserve uncertainty about milk transfer and medicinal dosing; do not convert case reports into a proven breast-milk harm pathway.

Assess milk supply and symptoms with qualified care; avoid infant remedies and respond immediately to poisoning or emergency signs.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record a product's ingredients, amount, timing, feeding concerns and symptoms for a clinical conversation. It cannot certify herbal safety, measure transfer into milk, diagnose poisoning or low supply, or decide when feeding should stop. Do not wait for a log or pattern when infant ingestion or emergency symptoms need care.

When to seek help

Avoid self-prescribed concentrated asafoetida while breastfeeding and never give a remedy to an infant. Seek immediate emergency advice for suspected infant remedy ingestion. Blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing difficulty, seizures, loss of consciousness or sudden throat swelling need emergency care immediately. Do not induce vomiting or use a home antidote. Do not automatically interrupt breastfeeding after an ordinary seasoned meal; obtain exposure-specific advice when needed.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Hing is a food flavouring and traditional remedy; concentrated preparations are different exposures from ordinary seasoning.
  • A milk-supply benefit and safe medicinal lactation dose are not established; obtain feeding support instead of relying on a remedy.
  • Direct infant ingestion has caused serious methemoglobinemia; this does not establish harm through breast milk after a seasoned meal.
  • Never give asafoetida remedies to babies. Suspected infant ingestion, breathing problems, blue lips, seizures or loss of consciousness require immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

What is asafoetida or hing?

It is a strongly scented dried Ferula gum-resin used in food and traditional remedies. Powders may contain other ingredients. Plant history and a food use do not establish safety for every extract, plant part or medicinal mixture.

Are its traditional health benefits proven?

Traditional digestive, respiratory, skin, neurological or reproductive claims are not established breastfeeding treatments. Laboratory findings are not proof of a safe effective remedy. Seek assessment for the condition rather than replacing prescribed care.

Can asafoetida increase breast milk?

Reliable evidence does not establish that benefit or a safe medicinal dose. A feeding assessment, milk removal, infant weight and age-appropriate nappies are more useful starting points; necessary supplemental nutrition must not be delayed.

Is medicinal asafoetida safe while breastfeeding?

Safety is insufficiently known, so avoid self-prescribed concentrated remedies and seek professional advice. The claim that milk transfer has been shown to cause infant bleeding is not established by the reviewed evidence. Lack of data is not proof of safety.

What if I ate food containing hing?

An ordinarily seasoned meal differs from a concentrated remedy. Do not automatically stop breastfeeding or discard milk. Obtain individual advice if the amount or ingredients are uncertain, a concentrated product was used, or parent or baby has symptoms.

Can I give it to my baby for colic?

No. Direct infant use has caused life-threatening methemoglobinemia, which affects oxygen delivery. Do not add it to milk or apply a preparation where the baby can swallow it. Seek emergency advice immediately after suspected remedy ingestion.

Could it interact with medicines or cause side effects?

Digestive or allergic symptoms are possible concerns, and product strength and interactions are uncertain. Ask a pharmacist, especially with blood thinners, blood-pressure or seizure treatment. Do not stop prescribed medicines or assume a different herb is safe.

Which symptoms need immediate help?

Blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing or swallowing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, seizures or loss of consciousness require immediate emergency care. Suspected infant ingestion of a remedy needs immediate emergency advice even without symptoms. Do not induce vomiting or give home antidotes.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
